To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the one-dimensional, planar solutions of the undercooled Stefan Problem in two dimensions are unstable with respect small perturbations transversal to the planar interface; (2) the resulting solutions generically develop cusp singularities at the blow up point, (3) the asymptotic behaviour near the cusp is given by a power law with a singularity of the form r-3/4, where r is the distance from the cusp.
the undercooled, one-phase, two-dimensional, planar Stefan problem admits blow-up behaviours that are unstable with respect, to small, transverse perturbations.

the undercooled Stefan Problem in two dimensions, with initial data that are planar and one-dimensional, and that exhibit undercooling Delta < 1, are generically unstable with respect to transversal perturbation, and that the solutions generated by the instability are cusped, in finite time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: What happens when we perturb the undercooled one-dimensional Stefan problem?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the undercooled, two-dimensional Stefan problem is not amenable to a simple description in terms of one-dimensional solutions.
the one-phase, two-dimensional Stefan problem with undercooling Delta < 1 exhibits a cusp in its interface, and that this behaviour is stable.
the undercooling of a planar interface is not a generic property, in the sense of Arnold.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cusp phenomenon is a natural consequence of the undercooling phenomenon in the Stefan problem.
the undercooled Stefan problems are not well-posed for N = 2 and Delta = 1.
the cusp formation is a robust phenomenon in the undercooled, two-dimensional Stefan problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the formation of a cusp, in the two-dimensional undercooled Stefan Problem, is not only possible, but it is in fact a generic feature of the solutions.
, in the presence of undercooling, the planar, one-phase Stefan problem exhibits a rich variety of behaviours, which are not present in the classical, one-phase problem.
undercooling can be used to control the formation of cusp singularities in the two-dimensional Stefan problem.
